newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Tight Asian storage space forces jet fuel westward.
newsitem.headline: Tight Asian storage space forces jet fuel westward.

text.p: Brimming storage tanks in Singapore and other Asian terminals has forced several oil trading firms and major oil companies to ship jet fuel cargoes to the U.S. West Coast, traders said on Tuesday.
They said the companies are shipping the products on a prayer that they might be sold into the U.S. domestic market or at worst be stored there until the Asian winter demand kicks in.

Storage tanks in major centres such as Singapore, Jebel Ali, Guam and China are all full of jet-kerosene fuel and gas oil as oil companies built up stocks due to poor prompt demand and a steep contango in the forward markets.
"I think that it (the shipments) would provide temporary relief to the storage," one trader said.
"But as the contango is wide it will be easily filled up again with barrels from the Middle East."

Traders said as soon as the excess jet fuel are cleared, their place would be filled by new production in Singapore, as well as by shipments from the Middle East, as regional demand continues to lag supply.
"For example, storage at Jebel Ali will be full till the end of the year and will be brought here by companies that have term barrels," the trader said.
In addition to Jebel Ali, some two million barrels of jet fuel are in storage in Singapore, and probabaly another 1.5 million barrels in Guam and China, traders said.

Singapore has a storage capacity of about three million cubic metres, 70 percent of which is for clean oil products such as gas oil, jet-kerosene fuel, gasoline and naphtha and the rest is dirty products such as fuel oil.
They said four jet fuel vessels from Singapore have been fixed for the U.S. West Coast ranging between 30,000 and 60,000 tonnes for end-August lifting.
The parties involved are a European major, a US refiner, a Swiss trader and a Dutch trader.
Traders said another European major is also initiating a shipment to the U.S. West Coast if the freight rates were attractive.

But they said this did not signal an opening of a floodgate westward, adding that those involved must make sure that buyers can be found within two months or they would be forced to bring the cargoes back East.
Some traders also said that not all the cargoes will actually make the long trip to the U.S. West Coast as some might end up in storage tanks in Guam, Hawaii or the Caribbean.
They said this week's American Petroleum Institute product inventory data due out later this evening would be a good indicator for sellers of arbitrage cargoes.
Traders said high stocks in this region have taken a toll on jet fuel values with offers stuck in a $23.00-$24.00 range, with a trade last Friday at $22.80. Jet fuel was valued near $25.00 in June.

They said a ray of hope is seen in the scheduled shutdown of Indonesia's 200,000-barrel-per-day crude distillation unit at Cilacap starting in early October for a three-month maintenance and upgrading works.

They said even though Indonesia's imports for September might be limited to less than 800,000 barrels, compared with two million barrels in July and 1.5 million in August, it could pick up again in October due to the shutdown.
Traders said if the turnaround of the large crude unit did extend to three months, Indonesia might seek additional jet fuel from Singapore.
But most of Indonesia's gas oil and jet fuel requirements would still be obtained from the Middle East, which would not help to alleviate the oversupply here, traders said.
